title: The prayer rope
hook: a knotted wool rope, one Jesus Prayer per knot

segments.voice: Yesterday, penthos: holy grief, tears that wash rather than wound. Your line was tears that wash.

A loop of black wool sits in a monk's hand. It isn't a string of beads. It's knots, each one tied by hand, close together, with a small woolen cross where the loop closes. His thumb finds a knot, and he says a short prayer. Then the next knot, another prayer. Nothing about it is fancy. It would fit in a coat pocket. You met the Jesus Prayer back on day ninety-nine; this is the thing in the hand that keeps it company. In Greek it's called a komboskini. In Russian it's chotki, and that's today's word.

Why knots at all? Paul tells the Thessalonians, in three words, "Pray without ceasing." For anyone who takes that at its word, a rope helps: a way to keep going without losing your place, or your attention. It's cheap, quiet and always to hand. There's a story about the knots. Tradition says a monk tied knots in a cord to count his prayers, and the devil kept coming in the night and untying them. So he was shown a new kind of knot, woven out of little crosses, that the devil couldn't undo. It's a legend, but it says plainly what the rope is for: a prayer, tied tight. The prayer itself is short. Its usual form asks the Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, to have mercy on me, a sinner, and its words echo the Gospels. A blind man by the road at Jericho shouts, "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." A tax collector in the temple won't even lift his eyes, and prays, "God be merciful to me a sinner." Put those two together and you can hear it. And the rope isn't a scoreboard. In this tradition the point is attention, not the total. The knot under the thumb brings a wandering mind back, gently, the way a friend's hand on your shoulder does. Lose your place, and you simply carry on from the next knot.

Tie a few knots, slowly, in whatever is at hand: a shoelace, a thread, a phone charger if that's all you've got. Hold it and let your thumb find one knot at a time; if you pray, say the Jesus Prayer once for each, and if you don't, take one breath for each, a single moment of attention. When your mind wanders, the next knot calls you back.
Chotki. The Orthodox prayer rope: knotted wool, one Jesus Prayer for each knot, and a thumb that keeps the place.
Your line: a knot, a prayer. The rope is for attention, not for counting. That's day one thousand one hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Orthodox monks and lay people pray the Jesus Prayer on a knotted wool rope, moving the thumb one knot for each prayer; in Greek it is called a komboskini, in Russian chotki.

chat.says: What's that knotted wool loop some Orthodox Christians carry around?
options: A prayer rope. Each knot is one short prayer, a way to keep attention, not keep score.
A scoreboard. Each knot marks a prayer, and the total shows how holy you are.
Jewelry. It's a monastery souvenir, worn for looks more than used for prayer.
chat.meaning: The chotki is the Orthodox prayer rope: one Jesus Prayer for each knot. The point is attention, not the total; the next knot brings a wandering mind back.

notes: The Jesus Prayer is described, not quoted ('asks the Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, to have mercy on me, a sinner'); confirm that rendering of the usual form is acceptable.
Knot legend given as 'tradition says' and 'a legend'; in some tellings an angel shows St Pachomius the knot. Left unnamed. Confirm.

Description of the rope (black wool, knots woven from small crosses, a woolen cross where the loop closes) is general; ropes vary in color and some have beads or tassels. No knot counts given on purpose.
Original: чётки (CHOT-kee, more exactly CHYOT-kee) and κομποσκοίνι (also spelled κομβοσκοίνι). Check spelling and transliteration 'komboskini'.
'In three words' counts 'Pray without ceasing' (KJV). 'Jericho' for Mark 10:46–47 is in the text.
'Nobody is counting but God, and God isn't keeping that kind of count' is a light line; check it doesn't read as speaking for God.

Editor pass: cut the unsourced history of why monks needed a rope; 'its roots are in the Gospels' softened to 'its words echo the Gospels'; cut the closing line that spoke for God ('God isn't keeping that kind of count') and ended on a concrete detail instead.

Audit: hook's garbled 'In Russian, and today's word: chotki' rewritten; fork reveal no longer says the rope is 'not to keep a tally', since the teach's own legend has a monk tying knots to keep count (ropes are also used to keep a rule of prayer).

Job 2 restyle: the hook now points back to day 99 (The Jesus Prayer) instead of 'we've already met'. Job 3: the Cyrillic чётки is left out of the gloss (the path's lint allows only Greek or Latin letters).
